metadata.source: Langdale & Lemire, Parsing Gigabytes of JSON per Second, VLDB Journal 28(6) 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.08318

text: Structural indexing for parsing: a first stage compares the input against each structural character with SIMD instructions, 32 or 64 bytes at a time, and converts the comparisons into bitmaps where a set bit marks a structural character. A second stage walks the bitmaps. SIMD combined with minimal branching sets speed records; branch-heavy loops over bit vectors in general purpose registers (Mison) are slower. Parsing reaches gigabytes per second per core.

metadata.source: minio/simdcsv and nullprogram.com/blog/2021/12/04 (Fast CSV processing with SIMD)

text: CSV with SIMD: stage one builds a quote mask and a separator mask; quoted regions come from a prefix XOR of the quote bits (carry-less multiplication, PCLMULQDQ), and separators inside quotes are cleared. Stage-one throughput is about 1.5 to 1.8 GB/s per core; full parsing around 1 GB/s per core.

metadata.source: Polychroniou & Ross, A comprehensive study of main-memory partitioning, SIGMOD 2014; Boncz et al. 1999

text: Partitioning fanout: best case is a fanout about the L1 TLB capacity, 64 on Intel CPUs. A larger fanout causes a TLB miss for nearly every tuple; a fanout near the cache set associativity causes conflict misses. Multi-pass radix partitioning limits the fanout of each pass to avoid TLB thrashing. Out-of-cache partitioning uses buffers and switches to in-cache partitioning with wider fanout for small parts.

metadata.source: Balkesen, Teubner, Alonso, Ozsu, Main-memory hash joins on multi-core CPUs, ICDE 2013

text: Hardware-conscious partitioning: software write-combining buffers of one cache line per partition, flushed with non-temporal stores, plus limiting the fanout of each partitioning pass to reduce TLB misses. Hardware-oblivious approaches win only in a narrow set of parameter combinations.

metadata.source: Leis, Boncz, Kemper, Neumann, Morsel-driven parallelism, SIGMOD 2014

text: Morsel-driven parallelism: small fragments of input (morsels) are scheduled to worker threads that run entire operator pipelines until the next pipeline breaker. Fine-grained run-time scheduling avoids load imbalance of static partitioning; fusing operators into one pipeline avoids materializing intermediate results between phases.

metadata.source: Crotty, Leis, Pavlo, Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your DBMS?, CIDR 2022

text: mmap file access: touching an unmapped page takes a page fault; evicting or unmapping pages requires TLB shootdowns, inter-processor interrupts to flush remote TLBs, which have a significant performance impact with many threads. mmap works well when the whole dataset fits in memory and is read only.

metadata.source: LKML 2013 huge page fault thread; kernel docs for MADV_POPULATE_READ/WRITE; LWN 2026 mmap_lock patches

text: Anonymous memory page faults: faulting 2MB huge pages is dominated by clearing (zeroing) each huge page. Prefaulting with MAP_POPULATE from many threads scales badly because of page table lock and mmap_lock contention; MADV_POPULATE_WRITE is the fastest way to prefault and allocate backing huge pages. Kernel time for fresh memory grows with thread count. Reusing already-faulted memory avoids both the fault and the zeroing.

metadata.source: arXiv 2602.15214 Decomposing Docker Container Startup Performance (2026); medium.com The Overhead of Docker Run; gvisor.dev performance guide

text: Container startup: a full docker run on native Linux costs hundreds of milliseconds (about 391 ms measured on Ubuntu; 568 ms on SSD in a 2026 study), dominated by runtime and daemon overhead rather than image size. This fixed cost is outside the program's control.

Transparent huge pages: the kernel mode is always, madvise or never. madvise only gives huge pages to regions marked with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE). Distributions differ in their default; container hosts may use always or madvise. An allocator that marks its arenas MADV_HUGEPAGE gets huge pages under both always and madvise, but not under never.

metadata.source: Neumann, Efficiently compiling efficient query plans for modern hardware, VLDB 2011 (data-centric pipelines)

text: Pipeline fusion: process each tuple through as many operators as possible while it is in registers and cache, materializing only at pipeline breakers. Each removed materialization saves a write and a read of the intermediate data and a phase barrier.

Thread scaling: 1 thread 8.69 s, 2 threads 4.56 s, 4 threads 3.21 s, 8 threads 3.25 s. Throughput stops growing at the physical core count. Kernel time 2.5 s at 1 thread, 9.6 s at 8 threads: kernel page fault and zeroing time grows with threads. Phase utilization is about 90 percent, so barriers and stragglers are not the limit.

Kernel time: reading all 1.53 GB of event input costs about 0.3 s of kernel time; the rest of the 2.5 s single-thread kernel time is page faults and zeroing of about 1.3 GB of fresh anonymous memory. Without transparent huge pages kernel time doubles and there are 500 thousand minor faults.
Fanout at 8 threads on 5M events: 4096 event-id and 2048 person buckets 0.70 s; 1024 and 512 buckets 0.57 s; 512 and 256 buckets 0.59 s; 256 and 128 buckets 0.64 s. Single thread unaffected.

metadata.where: scorer: Cascade Lake n2, 8 vCPU = 4 cores with hyperthreads, 24 GB

text: Scorer results: v3 2.16 s; 166c8eb 1.40 s; c6a8332 1.23 s; 988dfff 1.10 s; faeaf07 (fanout capped at 1024/512, 16-byte person records) 1.18 s. Local improvements of 12 percent at 8 threads did not appear on the scorer. Scores on the same machine vary a few percent and across machines up to 20 percent.

Profile: event parse loop 54 percent of instructions and 41 percent of last-level read misses; sessions about 20 percent; person bucket writes caused 21 percent of first-level write misses when staging lines exceeded L1. Bounds checks and pointer bookkeeping about 14 percent. About 1100 to 1300 cycles per event in total.
